title: Henselian projection kernels of a surjective nil-kernel ring tower
statement: Let $(A_n)_{n\geq1}$ be an inverse sequence of commutative unital rings with unital ring homomorphisms $A_{n+1}\to A_n$. Suppose every transition is surjective and every element of its kernel is nilpotent. Put $A=\varprojlim_n A_n$, the ring of compatible tuples with componentwise operations. For every $n\geq1$, the projection $\pi_n:A\to A_n$ is surjective. Write $I_n=\ker(\pi_n)$, so $A/I_n\simeq A_n$. Then $I_n$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $A$ (the intersection of its maximal ideals), and $(A,I_n)$ is a henselian pair [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology]. Explicitly, for every monic $f\in A[T]$ and factorization of its reduction $\bar f=g_nh_n$ into monic polynomials $g_n,h_n\in A_n[T]$ generating the unit ideal, there are monic $g,h\in A[T]$ reducing to $g_n,h_n$ such that $f=gh$. No nilpotence bound on the transition kernels, locality, Noetherian condition, or adic presentation is assumed.

source.place: Tag 0CT7 (lemma-limit-henselian), for a sequence indexed by positive integers; projection surjectivity by successive lifting in the surjective tower.

proof.text: Write $p_m:A_{m+1}\to A_m$ for the transitions and $p_{r,s}:A_r\to A_s$ for their composites. Fix $n$ and $b_n\in A_n$. Recursively choose $b_{m+1}$ with $p_m(b_{m+1})=b_m$ for $m\geq n$, using surjectivity; for $m<n$ set $b_m=p_{n,m}(b_n)$. These entries form a compatible tuple in $A$ projecting to $b_n$. Thus $\pi_n$ is surjective. The induced map $A/I_n\to A_n$ is injective by the definition of its kernel and surjective by this construction, hence is a ring isomorphism.

source.place: Tag 0CT7 (lemma-limit-henselian), proof, specialized to a sequence; elementary details expanded

proof.text: For $r>s$, every element of $\ker(p_{r,s})$ is nilpotent. Induct on $r-s$: the base is the hypothesis. If $x$ maps to zero in $A_s$, its image in $A_{r-1}$ is nilpotent by induction, so $x^e\in\ker(p_{r-1})$ for some $e\geq1$; the hypothesis gives $(x^e)^d=0$ for some $d\geq1$. This uses exponents depending on $x$. Also, if any $A_s$ is the zero ring then $1\in\ker(p_s)$ forces $A_{s+1}$ to be zero; earlier rings are zero by unitality and surjectivity. Hence all rings and $A$ are zero, and every assertion is immediate. In the remaining steps all $A_m$ and $A$ are nonzero.

source.place: Tag 0CT7 (lemma-limit-henselian), proof, specialized to a sequence; elementary details expanded

proof.text: If $a\in1+I_n$, then $a_m=1$ for $m\leq n$ and $a_m-1\in\ker(p_{m,n})$ for $m>n$. Step 2 makes $a_m-1$ nilpotent. If $z^e=0$, the identity $(1+z)\sum_{j=0}^{e-1}(-z)^j=1$ gives an inverse to $1+z$. Thus every $a_m$ is a unit. The inverses form a compatible tuple, since ring maps preserve inverses and inverses are unique. This tuple is an inverse of $a$ in $A$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-jacobson-radical-one-plus-units] to obtain $I_n\subseteq\operatorname{rad}(A)$.

source.place: Tag 0CT7 (lemma-limit-henselian), proof, specialized to a sequence; elementary details expanded

proof.text: We will preserve coprimality at each successive lift. Suppose monic $g_{m+1},h_{m+1}\in A_{m+1}[T]$ reduce to coprime $g_m,h_m\in A_m[T]$. Choose $u_m,v_m$ with $u_mg_m+v_mh_m=1$, and lift their finitely many coefficients along the surjection $p_m$, obtaining $u,v$. Then $q=ug_{m+1}+vh_{m+1}-1$ has all coefficients in $J_m=\ker(p_m)$, so lies in $J_mA_{m+1}[T]$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-locally-nilpotent-extension] to $A_{m+1}\to A_{m+1}[T]$: $q$ is nilpotent. The geometric-sum identity of step 3 makes $1+q$ a unit. Multiplying $u,v$ by its inverse gives a Bezout identity for $g_{m+1},h_{m+1}$.

source.place: Tag 0CT7 (lemma-limit-henselian), proof, specialized to a sequence; elementary details expanded

proof.text: Fix $f,g_n,h_n$ as in the statement and write $f_m$ for the coefficientwise image of $f$ in $A_m[T]$. Recursively construct pairs $(g_m,h_m)$ for $m\geq n$ with $f_m=g_mh_m$, both monic and generating the unit ideal, and $p_m(g_{m+1})=g_m$, $p_m(h_{m+1})=h_m$. The prescribed pair is the base case. Given the pair at $m$, use the isomorphism $A_{m+1}/J_m\simeq A_m$ and apply [lem-weil-pbc-henselian-factorization-locally-nilpotent] to $f_{m+1}$ and this factorization: its hypotheses hold because $J_m$ is a nil ideal and the factors at $m$ are monic and coprime. It supplies monic factors at $m+1$ with the prescribed reductions. Step 4 proves their coprimality, completing the induction. No uniqueness assertion is needed.

source.place: Tag 0CT7 (lemma-limit-henselian), proof, specialized to a sequence; elementary details expanded

proof.text: Put $d=\deg(g_n)$ and $e=\deg(h_n)$. A unital map between nonzero rings preserves the degree of a monic polynomial, since its leading coefficient stays $1$ and all higher coefficients stay zero. Consequently all $g_m$ have degree $d$ and all $h_m$ have degree $e$. For each coefficient index $i<d$, the compatible coefficients of $g_m$ for $m\geq n$ extend to a tuple in $A$ by applying transitions at the earlier indices. Denote this tuple $c_i$ and set $g=T^d+\sum_{i<d}c_iT^i$; define $h=T^e+\sum_{i<e}b_iT^i$ similarly. These are monic finite polynomials reducing to every chosen pair at $m\geq n$, and in particular to $g_n,h_n$. At every index $m\geq n$ their product projects to $f_m$; applying transitions gives the same equality for $m<n$. Each coefficient of $f-gh$ is therefore a tuple with all entries zero, hence is zero. Thus $f=gh$. This includes $d=0$ or $e=0$, with the corresponding sum empty.

source.place: Tag 0CT7 (lemma-limit-henselian), proof, specialized to a sequence; elementary details expanded

proof.text: Step 3 gives the Jacobson-radical condition. Steps 5 and 6 give every monic coprime-factorization lift over $A/I_n\simeq A_n$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-henselian-factorization-criterion], conditions (i) and (ii), to conclude that $(A,I_n)$ is henselian in the finite-algebra idempotent sense of [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology]. The construction already proves the explicit factorization clause, and step 1 supplies both the surjectivity and quotient identification for every $n$.
